name: Sechelt
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Accentuation in the Salish tongue is as marked as in English. But it has a wider syntactic and grammatic use than in our language. I have not yet satisfactorily determined in my own mind the basic principle of the accent in Salish. [...] But speaking broadly two main principles reveal themselves, viz., radix accentuation and quantity accentuation. Both these rules are frequently disregarded and the accent is shifted to some other syllable in the word for syntactic and rhetoric purposes. It is a common principle in the Salish dialects to distinguish homonymous terms by a shifting of the accent [...] Thus: sk·ṓmai, hair, and sk·omaí, dog; mEtcín, lice; and mḗtcin, testicles.
new_statements.citation: Hill-Tout, Charles. 1904. Report on the Ethnology of the Síciatl of British Columbia, a Coast Division of the Salish Stock. Journal of the Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland 34: 20-91.
new_statements.locator: p. 61, section 'Accent.' (scan leaf 74 of the archive.org volume in.ernet.dli.2015.104177); accent shift in reduplication p. 62
new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed position is given. The author says he cannot state the basic principle; accent tends to fall on the root ('radix accentuation') or to follow vowel quantity ('quantity accentuation'), but both tendencies are often overridden, accent can be moved for syntactic/rhetorical effect, and accent position alone distinguishes (near-)homonyms, i.e. it is at least partly lexical/contrastive. On p. 62 grammatical categories expressed by reduplication (diminutive, distributive etc.) are said to involve 'a shifting of the accent'. The modern authority (Beaumont 2011, seen only second-hand) adds that every word has at least one stressed syllable and some words carry stress on every syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing in Hill-Tout. Second-hand (Wikipedia < Beaumont 2011): some words have stress on every syllable; no primary/secondary distinction described.
new_statements.exceptions: Both stated tendencies 'are frequently disregarded'; accent shifted 'for syntactic and rhetoric purposes'; minimal pairs by accent (sk·ṓmai 'hair' vs sk·omaí 'dog'; mEtcín 'lice' vs mḗtcin 'testicles'); accent shift as an exponent of reduplicative categories (p. 62).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent on cited isolated words, but the author explicitly extends accent to 'syntactic and rhetoric' (phrase-level) uses; statement is framed for 'the Salish tongue' generally within the Síciatl (Sechelt) sketch, with Sechelt examples. Pre-phonemic 1904 transcription.
new_statements.identity_note: Hill-Tout's 'Síciatl' is Sechelt (sech1246); his consultants were Sechelt people (fieldwork c. 1902-03). The 'Accent' paragraph is worded about 'the Salish tongue'/'the Salish dialects' in general but stands inside the Síciatl grammatical sketch and is illustrated with Síciatl words. The modern authority (Beaumont 1985, 2011) describes the same language (speakers from Sechelt, B.C.) but could not be opened; its stress sentence is known only through Wikipedia's unpaged paraphrase.

sources.locator: p. 61, section 'Accent.' (scan leaf 74 of the archive.org volume in.ernet.dli.2015.104177); accent shift in reduplication p. 62
sources.note: p.61: accent is strongly marked; author has 'not yet satisfactorily determined' its basic principle; two broad tendencies, 'radix accentuation and quantity accentuation', both 'frequently disregarded', accent shifted for syntactic/rhetorical purposes; homonyms distinguished by accent position (sk·ṓmai 'hair' vs sk·omaí 'dog'; mEtcín 'lice' vs mḗtcin 'testicles'). p.62: reduplicative categories expressed partly 'by a shifting of the accent'.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Sechelt language' (raw wikitext, fetched sources 2026-09-17), section 'Stress and syllable structure', citing Beaumont 2011 Sechelt Dictionary (no page).
sources.note: Second-hand: 'All Sechelt words have at least one stressed syllable, but some words have stress on every syllable. This gives the language its characteristic "choppy" cadence.' Also notes /i/ -> [e] and devoiced schwa in unstressed syllables (cited to Beaumont 1985/2011).

sources.citation: UBC Working Papers in Linguistics ICSNL/ICSL archive index (lingpapers.sites.olt.ubc.ca/icsnl-volumes/), volumes 1966-2026, searched for Sechelt/shíshálh/Timmers/Beaumont and for stress-titled papers.
sources.note: Only five Sechelt papers exist in the archive (all fetched sources above); no paper on Sechelt stress in any volume (stress papers exist for Squamish, Halkomelem, Lushootseed, SENĆOŦEN, Sliammon/Comox acoustics, Lillooet, etc., but none for Sechelt).

sources.citation: Beaumont, Ronald C. 1977. Causation and control in Sechelt. Papers for the 12th ICSL (Omak, WA), 18 pp.
sources.note: Footnote 4 only: vowel of an unstressed suffix tends to reduce; '-naxw- is a stressed suffix in which [the vowel] is sometimes intensified' (cf. Hukari 1976:49). Implies morphologically governed stressed vs unstressed suffixes; no placement rule.
